description: §19.10.4 — the TWO limbs of E-TRANSACTION-CONTROL-FLOW that survive the S453 ruling. (1) A `yield` inside a `transaction { }`: a yield SUSPENDS the block rather than leaving it, so neither of §19.10.3's endings applies — rolling back would discard work the block is about to continue and committing would end a transaction that is still open. (2) A `return` inside an arm of a `match` inside the block: impl#1 lowers a match arm as a nested function (emitMatchExpr IIFE), so the exit returns from the ARM only and never reaches the block's commit-or-rollback — measured under a naive S453 implementation: the case compiled clean, the author's `return 5` was SWALLOWED, the post-`match` write RAN, and both rows persisted with no rollback (g-stmt-match-block-return-falls-through). ⚑ REWRITTEN AT S453: this case previously pinned the interim refusal of `return` and an outward `break`, which bryan RULED legal (they roll the block back) — those two shapes moved to ../transaction-control-flow-pos/ and to the runtime proof in ../../server-db/sql-transaction-exit-rollback-rt/. Two sites → exactly two diagnostics.
rationale: §19.10.4: "The compiler SHALL guarantee that every `transaction` block either commits (on success) or rolls back (on `fail` or SQL error). No transaction SHALL be left open." §19.10.3 names the block's endings as normal completion (COMMIT), `fail`, a SQL error and — since S453 — `return` / `break` / `continue` (ROLLBACK). A `yield` is none of them, and an exit inside a `match` arm reaches none of them.
